**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 71, verse 4:**

﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred, if only you knew.﴾ This sentence may be a justification (ta'lil) of His words ﴿and He will defer you until a specified term﴾, that is, a justification of the connection between the command and its reward, from His words ﴿that you worship Allah﴾ [Nuh: 3] through to His words ﴿and He will defer you until a specified term﴾, etc. This is because the connection between the command and its response implies, by its meaning: if you do not worship Allah, do not fear Him, and do not obey me, He will not forgive you and will not defer you until a specified term. So this connection and implication between this conditional that is implied and its consequence is justified by the sentence ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾. That is, the time that Allah has appointed for the descent of punishment upon you, if you do not worship Him and do not obey me, when its appointed time arrives while you persist in polytheism, faith will not benefit you at that time, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and its faith benefited it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time﴾ [Yunus: 98]. Therefore this serves as an exhortation to hasten to the worship of Allah and to fear Him.

The term (ajal) in His words ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾ is other than the term in His words ﴿and He will defer you until a specified term﴾. Consistent with this is His words after it, ﴿if only you knew﴾, which implies that they do not know this reality, which relates to the specified terms of the nations for their destruction. As for the non-deferment of the terms of lifespans when they arrive, this is known to people and is well established in the speech of the ancients. In the phrase "the term (ajal) of Allah" in His words ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾, by attributing (ajal) to the Name of Majesty (Allah), there is an indication that it is not the customary term, but rather a term which Allah has appointed for the people as a warning to them, so that they may believe in Allah.

It is also possible that the sentence is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from the specification of the end-point of their deferment until a specified term; that is, without their being deferred in a continuous manner. So the listener asks himself about the reason for limiting their deferment to another term. Thus, the term of Allah is other than the term in His words ﴿until a specified term﴾.

It is also possible that the sentence is a justification for both terms: the term understood from His words ﴿before there comes to them a painful punishment﴾ [Nuh: 1], for the word "before" (qabl) indicates that the punishment is fixed to a time that is not distant, so it has an indefinite term that is not far off; and the term mentioned in His words ﴿and He will defer you until a specified term﴾. Thus the term of Allah applies to the specified term, which is the term of each soul of the people.

Its attribution to Allah is an attribution of specification (idafat kashf), that is: the term which Allah has appointed and decreed for each individual.

By this you know that there is no contradiction between His words ﴿and He will defer you until a specified term﴾ and His words ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾, either because the intended meanings of the two words "term" (ajal) differ, in His words ﴿until a specified term﴾ and His words ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾; or because the two meanings of deferment differ in His words ﴿when it comes, is not deferred﴾. Thus the aspect of contradiction is removed.

As for the question of the deferment of terms, the increase and decrease in lifespans, and the unity of the term according to us, and the disagreement of the views of the Mu'tazila (a theological school) as to whether a person has one term or two terms, that is a different matter which is connected to two principles: the principle of divine knowledge of what will be, and the principle of Allah's decree of the causes and the sequence of their effects upon them.

As for what is in the knowledge of Allah, it does not change. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And no one is granted long life, nor is anything reduced from his lifespan, except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir: 11], that is, in the knowledge of Allah; and people do not have access to what is in the knowledge of Allah.

As for the existence of all the causes, such as the causes of life, and the sequence of their effects upon them, these change by Allah's bringing into being changers that did not exist before, as an honour to some of His servants or as a humiliation to others. In the hadith: "The charity of a Muslim man increases the lifespan," and it is a good, acceptable hadith. And from ʿAlī, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever wishes that his lifespan be extended, let him fear Allah and maintain the ties of kinship (silat al-rahim)," and its chain is good. So the terms of lifespans, determined by time or by the measure of the strength of the limbs and the proportion of their movement, are receptive to increase and decrease. As for the terms of divine punishments, which are determined by the occurrence of the deeds for which one is punished, within a short time or with a respite that cannot be deferred, these are what is meant by His words ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred﴾. Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes; and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39], according to the most apparent of the interpretations of it; and what is in the knowledge of Allah concerning that does not contradict what occurs in external reality.

So what Nuh encouraged his people to do is the cause of the deferment of their terms with Allah. If they did it, their terms would be deferred; and by the deferment of their terms it becomes clear that it was already established in the knowledge of Allah that they would do what Nuh called them to, and that their terms would be prolonged. And since they did not do it, it was revealed to the people that Allah knew they would not do what Nuh called them to, and that Allah would cut short their terms. This meaning has been indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created." The understanding of this has been difficult for many people, so they confused what is established in the knowledge of Allah with what the decree of Allah has manifested in external existential reality.

In the insertion of the verb (kuntum) before (ta'lamun) there is a notification that their acting in accordance with that, whose occurrence is negated, is the condition of the particle (law), and its non-occurrence is definitively established, as we have explained in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them?﴾ [Yunus: 2], in Surah Yunus.

The answer (jawab) of (law) is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿is not deferred﴾. The estimate is: "You would have been certain that it is not deferred."

The verb (qāla) is here left without the conjunction (al-'atf), because it introduces Noah's reply to God's words to him, ﴿Warn your people﴾ [Nuh: 1]. It is treated as the answer that follows a command immediately, in the manner of the dialogues mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah. (kullamā) is composed of two words: *kull* (every), a noun denoting the totality of the individual members of what it is attached to, and *mā* (*mā al-maṣdariyya*, the "verbal-*mā*," a particle that indicates the clause after it is equivalent to a verbal noun). Sometimes the time of the verbal noun's occurrence is meant by it, so they say *mā* is a temporal verbal *mā* (*ẓarfiyya maṣdariyya*), because it stands in for a noun of time.

The meaning is that they did not show any inclination to listen to his call, and they did not refrain for a moment from turning away and aversion from his call. For this reason he used the word (kullamā), which indicates that every one of his calls was accompanied by signs of turning away from it. This was already discussed under His saying, ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:20].

The object of (daʿawtuhum), "I called them," is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, namely His saying, ﴿that you worship Allah﴾ [Nūḥ 71:3].

The implied meaning is: "Whenever I called them to worship You, to fear You and to obey me in what I commanded them."

The *lām* in His saying (litaghfira), "that He may forgive," is the *lām* of causation (*lām al-taʿlīl*), meaning: I called them with the call to monotheism, which is the cause of forgiveness. So the call to it is motivated by forgiveness.

His saying ﴿whenever I called them﴾ is connected to the verb ﴿they put their fingers﴾ and is a temporal adverbial (*ẓarf zamān*).

The clause ﴿they put their fingers﴾ is the predicate of (inna), "indeed," and the connecting pronoun is the pronoun in (daʿawtuhum).

Putting the fingers in the ears prevents the sounds of speech from reaching the hearing.

The term "fingers" is used for the fingertips by way of metonymy (*majāz mursal*), with the relation of partness, because what is put into the ear is the fingertip, not the whole finger. He expressed the fingertips by "fingers" for emphasis, in wanting to block the hearing so that, if it were possible, they would have inserted all their fingers. This was discussed in His saying, ﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:19], in Surat al-Baqarah.

It is also permissible that it is a figurative depiction (*tamthīl*) of their state in turning away from accepting his speech and from seeing his station, by the state of one who stops his hearing with his fingertips and shields his eyes with the edge of his garment.

The call was made to be motivated by God's forgiveness of them, because it was a call to the cause of forgiveness, which is faith in God alone and obedience to His command through His Messenger.

In this there is an indirect allusion to their foolishness and an expression of wonder at their condition, since they turn away from a call that benefits them, whereas the right course required that they listen to it and reflect upon it.

*Al-iṣrār* is the firm determination to do an action. It is derived from *al-ṣarr*, which is tying something tightly and binding oneself to it. This was discussed under His saying, ﴿and they did not persist in what they did﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:135], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

The object of (aṣarrū), "they persisted," is omitted because it is evident, meaning: they persisted in what they were upon of polytheism.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 71, verses 8–12:

﴿Then indeed I called them openly.﴾ ﴿Then indeed I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them in private, a private speaking.﴾ ﴿So I said: "Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed He is ever Forgiving."﴾ ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain.﴾ ﴿And will provide you with wealth and sons, and will make for you gardens and will make for you rivers.﴾ He advanced in his complaint and his excuse that his call had been varied in its states in speech, between open and private. So the conjunction of the speech with (thumma) ("then"), which, in its conjoining of sentences, indicates that the content of the conjoined sentence is more important than the content of the one conjoined to it, because the variation in the manner of the call is more closely attached to the call than the times of its delivery; for the state is more intimately connected with its bearer than the time is with him. He mentioned that he called them openly, that is, publicly.

"Jihar" (openly) is a verbal noun of jahara, and here it is a description of the verbal noun of ﴿I called them﴾ [Nuh: 7], that is, a call openly.

Then he advanced, mentioning that he combined the open and the private, because combining the two states is stronger in the call and more forceful than singling out one of them. His saying ﴿I proclaimed to them﴾ is an emphasis of his saying ﴿I called them openly﴾, mentioned so that the conjunction ﴿and I spoke to them in private, a private speaking﴾ may be built upon it.

The meaning is that he sought what he thought would penetrate their hearts most of the attributes of the call: he called openly when openness is more beneficial, such as in gatherings of the common people, and he spoke privately to those whom he thought were avoiding the blame of their people for attending to hear his call. Thus the pronouns of the third person in his saying ﴿I called them﴾ and his saying ﴿I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them in private﴾ are distributed among the various kinds of people.

"Jihaaran" is in the accusative by substitution for the absolute object specifying the type of the call.

"Israran" is in the accusative as an absolute object serving for emphasis, that is, a hidden private speaking.

The reason for emphasizing the private speaking is that the private call was during his calling to their leaders and chiefs, because they were offended by their call being publicized in the hearing of their followers.

He detailed his call with the fa' of sequence, saying ﴿So I said: "Ask your Lord for forgiveness"﴾. This saying is what he said to them by night and by day, openly and privately.

The meaning of ﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness﴾ is: believe with a belief that will be a seeking of forgiveness for your sins, for if you do so, God will forgive you.

He gave as the reason for this to them that God is described with forgiveness as a constant attribute, which God has pledged to His servants who seek forgiveness. So the particle (inna) indicates the causal link, and the use of the verb (kāna) indicates the constancy of the attribute of God. And by the intensive form in His saying "Ever Forgiving" He indicates the completeness of His forgiveness.

This is a promise of the good of the Hereafter, and it is followed by a promise of the good of this world by way of the answer to the command, which is ﴿He will send the sky upon you﴾, and so on.

They were people of agriculture, so He promised them the descent of rain, by which comes safety from drought and an increase in wealth.

"Al-sama'" (the sky) here means rain, and among the names of rain is al-sama'. In the hadith of the Muwatta' and the two Sahihs, from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ led us in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyya following a rain that had fallen during the night," and so on. Mu'awiya ibn Malik ibn Ja'far said:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

"Midrar" means abundant in flow and pouring, and it is the flowing; it is said: "the sky poured forth with rain," and "a sky of midrar."

The meaning of that is that some rains follow others.

"Midrar" is of the intensive pattern, and this pattern is rarely joined by the feminine marker, as in the saying of Sahl ibn Malik al-Fazari:

"He became fond of a free woman, fragrant with perfume."

Therefore the ta' was not attached here, although the noun "sama'" is feminine.

"Al-irsal" (sending) is used metaphorically for conveying and giving, and its being transitive with (ʿalaykum) is because it is a conveying from above, like His saying ﴿and He sent upon them birds in flocks﴾ [al-Fil: 3].

"Amwal" is the plural of "mal," which includes every gain a person spends in acquiring what he needs.

By "gardens" in His saying ﴿and will make for you gardens﴾ is meant palm trees and grapevines, because gardens need irrigation.

The repetition of the verb (yaj'al) after the conjunctive waw in His saying ﴿and will make for you rivers﴾ is for emphasis, showing concern for the matter of the conjoined, because rivers are the support of gardens and water the fields and livestock.

This indicates that God rewards His righteous servants with a good life. He, exalted, said ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and He said ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the sky and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], and He said ﴿And that if they remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16].

So the conjunction of the speech with (thumma) ("then"), which, in its conjoining of sentences, indicates that the content of the conjoined sentence is more important than the content of the one conjoined to it, because the variation in the manner of the call is more closely attached to the call than the times of its delivery; for the state is more intimately connected with its bearer than the time is with him. He mentioned that he called them openly, that is, publicly.

"Jihar" (openly) is a verbal noun of jahara, and here it is a description of the verbal noun of ﴿I called them﴾ [Nuh: 7], that is, a call openly.

Then he advanced, mentioning that he combined the open and the private, because combining the two states is stronger in the call and more forceful than singling out one of them. His saying ﴿I proclaimed to them﴾ is an emphasis of his saying ﴿I called them openly﴾, mentioned so that the conjunction ﴿and I spoke to them in private, a private speaking﴾ may be built upon it.

The meaning is that he sought what he thought would penetrate their hearts most of the attributes of the call: he called openly when openness is more beneficial, such as in gatherings of the common people, and he spoke privately to those whom he thought were avoiding the blame of their people for attending to hear his call. Thus the pronouns of the third person in his saying ﴿I called them﴾ and his saying ﴿I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them in private﴾ are distributed among the various kinds of people.

"Jihaaran" is in the accusative by substitution for the absolute object specifying the type of the call.

"Israran" is in the accusative as an absolute object serving for emphasis, that is, a hidden private speaking.

The reason for emphasizing the private speaking is that the private call was during his calling to their leaders and chiefs, because they were offended by their call being publicized in the hearing of their followers.

He detailed his call with the fa' of sequence, saying ﴿So I said: "Ask your Lord for forgiveness"﴾. This saying is what he said to them by night and by day, openly and privately.

The meaning of ﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness﴾ is: believe with a belief that will be a seeking of forgiveness for your sins, for if you do so, God will forgive you.

He gave as the reason for this to them that God is described with forgiveness as a constant attribute, which God has pledged to His servants who seek forgiveness. So the particle (inna) indicates the causal link, and the use of the verb (kāna) indicates the constancy of the attribute of God. And by the intensive form in His saying "Ever Forgiving" He indicates the completeness of His forgiveness.

This is a promise of the good of the Hereafter, and it is followed by a promise of the good of this world by way of the answer to the command, which is ﴿He will send the sky upon you﴾, and so on.

They were people of agriculture, so He promised them the descent of rain, by which comes safety from drought and an increase in wealth.

"Al-sama'" (the sky) here means rain, and among the names of rain is al-sama'. In the hadith of the Muwatta' and the two Sahihs, from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ led us in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyya following a rain that had fallen during the night," and so on. Mu'awiya ibn Malik ibn Ja'far said:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

"Midrar" means abundant in flow and pouring, and it is the flowing; it is said: "the sky poured forth with rain," and "a sky of midrar."

The meaning of that is that some rains follow others.

"Midrar" is of the intensive pattern, and this pattern is rarely joined by the feminine marker, as in the saying of Sahl ibn Malik al-Fazari:

"He became fond of a free woman, fragrant with perfume."

Therefore the ta' was not attached here, although the noun "sama'" is feminine.

"Al-irsal" (sending) is used metaphorically for conveying and giving, and its being transitive with (ʿalaykum) is because it is a conveying from above, like His saying ﴿and He sent upon them birds in flocks﴾ [al-Fil: 3].

"Amwal" is the plural of "mal," which includes every gain a person spends in acquiring what he needs.

By "gardens" in His saying ﴿and will make for you gardens﴾ is meant palm trees and grapevines, because gardens need irrigation.

The repetition of the verb (yaj'al) after the conjunctive waw in His saying ﴿and will make for you rivers﴾ is for emphasis, showing concern for the matter of the conjoined, because rivers are the support of gardens and water the fields and livestock.

This indicates that God rewards His righteous servants with a good life. He, exalted, said ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and He said ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the sky and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], and He said ﴿And that if they remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 71, verses 13–14:

﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not attribute to Allah dignity? And He has created you in stages.﴾ He changed his address to his people from the manner of advice and command to the manner of rebuke, with His saying ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not attribute to Allah dignity?﴾

This is an interrogative whose form is that of a question about a matter that is established for them, in a state in which they do not hope to ascribe dignity (tawqir) to Allah.

The purpose is that there is nothing that can be established for them that would divert them from honouring Allah, so there is no excuse for you in not honouring Him.

The clause ﴿you do not hope﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun of those addressed, and the phrase "what is [the matter] with you" (ma laka) and its like is always accompanied by a circumstantial phrase after it, as in ﴿What is [the matter] with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49].

There has been disagreement about the meaning of His saying ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not attribute to Allah dignity?﴾ and about how its complements relate to their governing elements, giving rise to several opinions. Some of them keep the meaning of "hope" (raja') in its well-known sense, which is awaiting an outcome, and likewise keep the meaning of "dignity" (waqar) in its customary sense, which is greatness that calls for reverence. Others return to an interpretation of the meaning of "hope," others to an interpretation of the meaning of "dignity." From the combination of taking the apparent meaning and interpreting, it follows that the interpretation may apply to both, or to one of them while the other is kept in its apparent meaning.

On taking "hope" in its familiar, apparent meaning and likewise "dignity," Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Ibn Kaysan said: "What is [the matter] with you that you do not hope for reward from Allah, nor fear His punishment," meaning: so that you would worship Him, hoping that He would reward you for your worship and your honouring Him. This interpretation tends toward there being an elision (iktifa') in the speech, meaning: "and you do not fear His punishment." The point of the elision by means of the expression of surprise at their not hoping for reward is that this is what the people of right guidance and piety ought to aim for. To this meaning the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) referred when he began with his saying: "What is [the matter] with you that you are not in a state in which you hope for Allah's magnification of you in the abode of reward?"

This implies that the speech is an allusive metonymy (kinaya talwihiyya) urging them to believe in Allah, which entails hoping for His reward and fearing His punishment, because whoever hopes for Allah's magnification of him believes in Him, worships Him, and does righteous deeds.

On interpreting the meaning of "hope," Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the meaning of ﴿you do not hope﴾ is "you are not concerned with Allah's greatness." Qutrub said: this is a Hijazi usage of Mudar, Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, who say, "I did not raja'," meaning "I was not concerned." Al-Walibi and al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the meaning of ﴿you do not hope﴾ is "you do not know." Mujahid also said: "you do not see." It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about it, and he answered that raja' here means khawf (fear), and he recited the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

When the bees sting him, he does not hope for their sting,
and he has made a pact with them in a house of nub, honey-combs.

That is: he does not fear their sting, and he persists in gathering honey. Al-Farra' said: "raja'" is only used in the place of "khawf" because with hope there is a trace of fear of people, and for this reason "khawf" is used with the meaning of "knowledge," as in His saying ﴿And if you fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], and so on. The meaning is: you do not fear the greatness of Allah and His power to punish.

On interpreting "dignity," Qatadah said: "waqar" means "consequence" ('aqibah). That is: what is [the matter] with you that you do not hope for a consequence from Allah, that is, the consequence of faith; that is, the speech is a metonymy for rebuke for their abandoning belief in Allah. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani took waqar to mean "steadfastness" (thabat), and said: from this is His saying ﴿And remain in your houses﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], meaning "remain," and the meaning is: what is [the matter] with you that you do not establish the oneness of Allah?

From these two interpretations other meanings are composed, depending on whether "dignity" is ascribed in the sentence to its agent or to its object, and these are not hidden.

As for His saying "to Allah" (li-Allah), the more apparent view is that it is connected to "you hope" (tarjuna). It is permissible, in some of the earlier interpretations, for it to be connected to "dignity" (waqaran), either as the connection of the agent of a verbal noun to its verbal noun, in which case the lam in "li-Allah" is the lam of resemblance to ownership (lam shibh al-milk), meaning: the dignity which is Allah's disposal over His creation, should He wish to grant you dignity, that is, honour you with bliss; or as the connection of the object of a verbal noun, meaning: that you should honour Allah and fear Him, and not be negligent of His matter with the negligence of one who does not fear Him, in which case the lam is the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah).

The clause ﴿and He has created you in stages﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "to you" (lakum) or to the pronoun in "you hope," meaning: in a state in which you are certain that He created you in stages.

As for His having created them, this necessitates acknowledging His greatness, because He is their Fashioner and Maker, so it is incumbent upon them to acknowledge His majesty.

As for the fact that their creation is in stages, this is because the stages that they know of indicate His gentleness toward them in that process of development, and that is an allusion to their ingratitude for the blessing. Also, because the stages indicate the wisdom, knowledge and power of the Creator, for the development of creation from the stage of the sperm-drop to the stage of the foetus, to the stage of emerging as an infant, to the stage of childhood, to the stage of reaching maturity, to the stage of old age, and the coming of death upon life, and the stage of decay upon bodies after death, all of that while the essence is one, is a proof of the Creator's power over the modes of creation and transformation through the stages. They perceive this with the slightest attentiveness of mind, so they were deserving of arriving through it at knowledge of Allah's greatness and anticipating His punishment, because the indication of that is established within themselves. Is disposing of them by punishment and reward anything other than a lesser disposal than disposing of them by existence and annihilation?

"Atwar" is the plural of tawr, with a fatha and then a sukun. Tawr means "time" (tara), that is, an occurrence, which is an instance of actions or of times. So what is meant here by "atwar" is what occurs in instances and times of differing states, because what is intended by the multiplicity of instances and times is only the multiplicity of what occurs in them. It is a multiplicity by kind, not by repetition, as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

If he recovers, his blindness has lasted long,
and a man is created stage after stage.

"Atwaran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun of those addressed, meaning: in the stages of their creation, because "atwaran" has come to mean "states in stages."

﴿Have you not considered how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp?﴾ If this is part of Noah's (peace be upon him) speech to his people, as the exegetes (*mufassirun*) have understood it, then it is a transition from rebuke and allusion to argument for God's existence, His oneness and His power, using the signs found within themselves, and then turning to the signs found in the world. This is because of what you know of the indication in His words ﴿And He has created you in stages﴾ [Nuh: 14], which carries a reminder of blessings and establishes proof. He then transitions from this to mentioning another proof. He had already directed them to reflect on themselves first, because that is what is closest to what they perceive and feel, and then to reflect on the world and the wondrous things arranged within it that bear witness to the Creator, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful.

If it is instead an address from God Most High to the community, which the context of the surah permits through the lesson drawn from the states of past nations, which resemble the states of the polytheists, then this statement is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) for the sake of relevance (*munasaba*).

The *hamza* in (*a-lam tarawu*) is an interrogative of affirmation (*istifham taqriri*), used metaphorically to express denial of ignorance of the proofs of what they see.

The seeing (*ru'ya*) is visual. It could also be cognitive, meaning "Do you not know," in which case what is seen of this is included. (*Kayfa*) is in the accusative as the object of (*tarawu*). Here (*kayfa*) is stripped of the interrogative sense and purely indicates the manner, i.e., the state.

The meaning is: Do you not see the form and state of God's creation of the heavens?

The "heavens" here are orbits (*madarat*), meaning the planets, since each planet has an orbit which may itself be its heaven.

His words ﴿seven heavens﴾ may mean that the description "seven" was known to the addressees, the people of Noah, or to the community of the Islamic call, because they had known this beforehand; in that case it falls within the scope of (*a-lam tarawu*). It may also be a teaching to the addressees by way of incorporation (*idmaj*). Perhaps they were forerunners of the Chaldeans in this.

(*Tibaqan*): some of them are higher than others. This implies that they are separated from one another, and that some are higher than others, whether they are touching or whether there is between them what is called void (*khala'*).

[Page 203]

His words ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ can refer to the moon as one of the heavens, meaning the planets according to the older terminology based on observation. This is because the locative (*zarfiyya*) of (*fi*) denotes the enclosed thing being within a container like a vessel, and it also denotes a thing being among its group, as in the hadith of intercession: "and this community will remain therein with its hypocrites," and the saying of al-Numayri:

It was perfumed with musk, the valley of Nu'man, when Zaynab walked through it among modest women.

The moon is situated in the heaven that touches the earth, which is called the lowest heaven. God knows best their distances.

His words ﴿and made the sun a lamp﴾ are with the implicit meaning: "and made the sun therein a lamp." The sun is one of the planets.

Describing the moon as "light" is an intensive expression of its illumination, comparable to describing it with the verbal noun. The moon's light illuminates the earth with a beneficial illumination, unlike other stars of the night, whose illumination does not benefit mankind.

The *siraj* is a bright lamp whose light is kindled with a wick in oil, its flame regulated by the amount of oil remaining that covers it.

Describing the sun in this way is an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), in which the purpose is to bring the thing compared closer to the hearer's comprehension. The *siraj* was the most that one could use for illumination at night, and few Arabs possessed one. They used to see it only in the monasteries of monks or the palaces of kings and their likes. Imru' al-Qays said:

Its radiance shines, or the lamps of a monk, who tilts the wicks with pressed oil.

They described the palace of Ghumdan as lit at night along the road.

The sun is not described with *diya'* (radiance) as in the verse of Surat Yunus: ﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance﴾ [Yunus: 5]. The meaning is the same, which is illumination. Perhaps the choice of *siraj* here is to approximate the expression of Noah in his language, along with what it contributes regarding the verse-ending (*fasila*), because the verse-endings before it come on sound consonants. If it were said *diya'*, the verse-ending would become a *hamza*, and the *hamza* is close to the weak letters, so pausing on it would be heavy.

In describing the moon as "light" there is an allusion that the moon's light is not from its own essence, for the moon is dark, and it is illuminated only by the reflection of the sun's rays on the face that receives them, varying according to the differing degrees of that reception, partial or full. This is the effect of its appearing as a crescent, then the expansion of its luminosity until it becomes a full moon, then the withdrawal of that. During these states it lights the earth until it reaches the dark of the moon (*mahaq*). In contrast, the sun is described as a lamp because it is blazing, and its lights are essential to it, emanating from it to the earth and to the moon, like the lights of a lamp that fill the house and make the silver vessels and similar things in the house that face it shine.

The words ﴿and made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp﴾ combine argument and favour.

﴿Have you not considered how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp?﴾ If this is part of Noah's (peace be upon him) speech to his people, as the exegetes (*mufassirun*) have understood it, then it is a transition from rebuke and allusion to argument for God's existence, His oneness and His power, using the signs found within themselves, and then turning to the signs found in the world. This is because of what you know of the indication in His words ﴿And He has created you in stages﴾ [Nuh: 14], which carries a reminder of blessings and establishes proof. He then transitions from this to mentioning another proof. He had already directed them to reflect on themselves first, because that is what is closest to what they perceive and feel, and then to reflect on the world and the wondrous things arranged within it that bear witness to the Creator, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful.

If it is instead an address from God Most High to the community, which the context of the surah permits through the lesson drawn from the states of past nations, which resemble the states of the polytheists, then this statement is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) for the sake of relevance (*munasaba*).

The meaning is: Do you not see the form and state of God's creation of the heavens?

The "heavens" here are orbits (*madarat*), meaning the planets, since each planet has an orbit which may itself be its heaven.

His words ﴿seven heavens﴾ may mean that the description "seven" was known to the addressees, the people of Noah, or to the community of the Islamic call, because they had known this beforehand; in that case it falls within the scope of (*a-lam tarawu*). It may also be a teaching to the addressees by way of incorporation (*idmaj*). Perhaps they were forerunners of the Chaldeans in this.

(*Tibaqan*): some of them are higher than others. This implies that they are separated from one another, and that some are higher than others, whether they are touching or whether there is between them what is called void (*khala'*).

ﵟ"And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth" ﵞ﻿ ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth, a growth﴾ ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth, a [sure] bringing forth.﴾

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on verses 17–18 of Surah Nuh:

The argument from the creation of the heavens brought the earth into the imagination, so Nuh followed it with his previous argument, reasoning from the most wondrous of what they see of the states of what is upon the earth, namely the state of death and burial. He prepared for this with what precedes it, the creation of mankind.

In the course of this he also incorporated teaching them that man is created from the elements of the earth like plants, and informing them that after death there is another life.

The verb anbatakum ("caused you to grow") is used in the sense of anshaakum ("created you"), because of the resemblance between the creation of man and the growing of plants, in that both are a form of bringing into being, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He caused her to grow a good growth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], meaning, He brought her into being. This is also like the saying: "May God make you grow well (zara'aka Allah lil-khayr)." The resemblance is made closer here by the fact that the creation of man is composed of the elements of the earth. It has also been said that the estimate is: He caused your origin to grow, that is, Adam (peace be upon him), as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59].

Nabatan ("a growth") is a noun from anbata, treated as a verbal noun, so it occurs as an absolute object of (anbatakum) for emphasis. It was not formed on the regular pattern of its verb, so one does not say *inbatan*, because nabatan is lighter; since it could be used, and it is a eloquent usage, one did not turn away from it to the heavier form, for the sake of perfection in eloquence. This is unlike his saying after it (ikhraja, "bringing forth"), for one did not turn away from it to kharuja, because it does not harmonize with the rhyme-endings before it, which are built on an alif like the alif of ta'sis. Just as breaking these in the rhyme is counted a fault, so keeping to them in the rhymed prose (saj') and the verse-endings (fawasil) is counted a perfection.

The warning of resurrection has been incorporated within the argument. And because it is the more important rank than arguing against them from the basic fact of creation, the clause is joined by thumma ("then"), which indicates a rank-based delay, in His saying ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth, a [sure] bringing forth﴾. The intended object of the clause is the act of "and bring you forth," while His saying "then He will return you" is a preparation for it.

He emphasized (yukhrijukum, "bring you forth") with the absolute object to refute their denial of resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 71, verses 19–20:

﴿And Allah has made for you the earth a spread-out carpet﴾ ﴿that you may traverse therein broad roads﴾. This is an argument and an expression of favour. For this reason, the prepositional phrase "for you" (lakum), which marks purpose (lam al-ta'lil), is attached to the verb "made" (ja'ala), meaning: for your sake.

Al-bisat (carpet) is that which is spread out to sleep on and to sit on, whether a cloth or a rug. Thus, describing the earth as a carpet (bisat) is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), meaning: like a carpet. The point of resemblance is the suitability of the earth's surface through the evenness of its parts, such that it does not wound the feet of those who walk nor disturb the sides of those who lie down. The meaning is not that Allah made the volume of the earth like a carpet, since the earth's volume is spherical; he has alerted to this by the motivating cause in His saying "for you" (lakum) and by the final cause in His saying ﴿that you may traverse therein﴾. From the combination of the two causes arises an indication of all the blessings that people obtain from the levelling of the earth's surface, such as tilling and planting, and of a blessing specifically mentioned, namely travel across the earth, which was singled out for mention because it is the most important, since all people share in benefiting from it.

Al-subul (sing. sabil) is the plural of sabil, meaning the path. That is: that you may take for yourselves paths across the earth by which you are guided on your journeys.

Al-fijaj is the plural of fajj, and the fajj is the wide road. It is most commonly applied to a road between two mountains, because it is wider than the ordinary road.

﴿Noah said: "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children have increased him only in loss. And they have plotted a great plot. And they have said: 'Do not abandon your gods, and do not abandon Wadd, or Suwa', or Yaghuth, or Ya'uq, or Nasr.'"﴾

This sentence is a *badal* (substitution) for the sentence ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have called my people"﴾ [Noah: 5], as a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion), because the report of their disobedience to him is included in the report that he called them. It is possible that the two statements were made at one time, when Noah withdrew to privately address his Lord in reply to His command to him, ﴿Warn your people before a painful punishment comes to them﴾ [Noah: 1]. In that case, the repetition of the verb (*qala*, "he said") is of the type of mentioning the governing element of the substituted term in the substitution, as in God's words, ﴿It will be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114], to link his two statements, since the separation between them is long.

It is also possible that the two statements were made at two different times, and the Qur'an gathered them together as a report of his two replies to his Lord. In that case, the repetition of the verb (*qala*) is for the reasons we have mentioned, together with an indication of the distance between the two statements.

It is also permissible for the sentence to be a *isti'naf bayani* (explanatory resumption), because what precedes it, from His words ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have called my people"﴾ [Noah: 5] up to this point, arouses wonder at the condition of his people as related, so that the listener asks about the final outcome of their affair. Thus the mention of that is begun with this sentence and what follows it up to His words "helpers" (*ansaran*). The postponement of this statement after His words ﴿"My Lord, I have called my people night and day"﴾ [Noah: 5] is a progression in complaint about them, because this is a report of the occurrence of their disobedience after he had first presented the admonition to them with His words ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Noah: 11] up to His words ﴿broad roads﴾ [Noah: 20].

The name (*Nuh*, "Noah") is stated with the second statement rather than being replaced by a pronoun, because the referent of the pronoun would be too distant if the verb carried it. This report is used for what necessarily follows from its meaning, as was previously mentioned in His words ﴿He said: "My Lord..."﴾. The emphasis of the report with (*inna*) is for the sake of attention to what it is used to express, namely grief and seeking help.

Then He mentioned that they took up the words of those who prevented them from accepting Noah's call, that is, they followed their chiefs and leaders. He turned away from describing them as "the great ones" and the like to the relative pronoun, because the relative clause indicates their insolence in response to God's blessing upon them in wealth and children. Thus they turned the blessing, in their own view, into a cause of loss and misguidance.

Included in the relative clause is that they were people of wealth and children, as a hint that this was the reason their words were effective among their people and the people obeyed their orders. Their wealth, when they spent it to win over their followers, as God said, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of God﴾ [al-Anfal: 36]; and their children, whom they used to terrify those who opposed them.

The meaning is: they followed the people of wealth and children, whose wealth and children increased them only in loss, because they used them to support disbelief and corruption, and so they increased them in loss. For had they not had wealth or children, they would have been less inclined to commit corruption. God said, ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

*Khasar* (loss) is used figuratively for the occurrence of evil through means that are ordinarily a cause of good, like the loss of a merchant who sought profit. Since these people were losers, those who follow them will be like them in loss, while they think that they have guided them to success.

The referent of (*man*, "one who") is a group of the people, namely the people of wealth and children, who became more insolent because of it and did not give thanks. They were their chiefs. For this reason the plural pronoun is returned to it in His words ﴿and they plotted﴾, and His words ﴿and they said﴾, and His words ﴿and they have led many astray﴾ [Noah: 24].

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read (*wa-waladuhu*, "and his child") with a *fatha* on the *waw* and a *fatha* on the *lam*. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (*wa-wulduhu*) with a *damma* on the *waw* and a sukun on the *lam*. As for *walad*, with a *fatha* on the *waw* and a *fatha* on the *lam*, it is a noun applied to one child and to children collectively, so it is a noun of genus. As for *wuld*, with a *damma* and then a sukun, it is said to be a dialectal variant of *walad*, in which the singular and plural are the same, like *fulk*. It is also said to be the plural of *walad*, like *usud* being the plural of *asad*.

*Makr* (plotting) is concealing an action or a plan intended to harm another. That is, they plotted against Noah and those who believed with him, by secretly plotting against them so that they would fall into harm. It is said that they devised a stratagem to kill Noah and to incite the people against him and his followers.

*Kubbaran* is an intensive form, meaning "very great." It occurs in this pattern in a few words, such as *tuwwal*, meaning "very long"; *'ujjab*, meaning "very wondrous"; *husson*, *jummal*, meaning "very beautiful"; *qurra'*, meaning "one who recites much"; and *wuddha'*, meaning "one who is very bright/handsome." 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: this is a Yemeni dialect.

﴿And they said: "Do not abandon your gods, and do not abandon Wadd or Suwa'..."﴾ etc. That is, some of them said to others: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr are the idols of the people of Noah.

[p. 208]

By this you know that their names do not follow the derivations of Arabic words. In the *waw* of (*wadd*) there are two dialects among the Arabs: some of them put a *damma* on the *waw*, and Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read it that way; others put a *fatha* on the *waw*, and the rest read it so.

al-Bukhari transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr were names of righteous men of the people of Noah. When they died, Satan inspired their people to set up at their assemblies, where they used to sit, idols (*ansab*), and to name them after them. They did so, but they were not worshipped until those men died and knowledge was forgotten, and then they were worshipped. And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: they were the names of five sons of Adam (peace be upon him), who were worshippers. And from al-Mawardi: *Wadd* was the first idol to be worshipped.

The verse implies that these *ansab* were worshipped before the Flood. Some exegetes have said that these idols were erected for some of the righteous descendants of Adam, and some have said that they were idols between the time of Adam and the time of Noah.

This does not agree with the occurrence of the Flood, since it must have washed them away, and mankind was freed from polytheism after the Flood. It also does not agree with the existence of these names among the Arab tribes until the time of the Muhammadan mission (ﷺ). For in Dawmat al-Jandal, in the land of Kalb, there was an idol named Wadd. It is said that it was in the form of a man, made of brass and lead, and that it was in the form of a woman. Hudhayl had an idol named Suwa'. Murad and Ghutayf (with a *ghayn* and a *ta'*, a clan of Murad in al-Jawf near Saba') had an idol named Yaghuth. It was also among Ghatafan, and An'um and A'la, who are from Tayy, and the people of Jarash from Madhhij, took it and brought it to Murad, and they worshipped it. Then the Banu Najiyah tried to remove it from A'la and An'um, so they fled with it to al-Husayn, brother of the Banu al-Harith of Khuza'ah. Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: I saw Yaghuth made of lead; they used to carry it on a camel that was *ahrad* (with a *ha'*, meaning one that paws with its forelegs when walking), and they would travel with it and not provoke it, until it was the one that knelt. When it knelt they would dismount and say: "It has approved the place for you," and they would pitch a tent around it and dwell around it.

Yaghuth was in the form of a lion.

Hamdan had an idol named Ya'uq, which was in the form of a horse. Kahlan of Saba' had it, and then his descendants inherited it until it came to Hamdan.

[p. 209]

Himyar and Dhu al-Kala' among them had an idol named Nasr, in the form of a vulture among birds. This is transmitted in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the idols that were among the people of Noah went to the Arabs. End of quote. So it is possible that they were transferred with their very identities, and it is possible that the Arabs named them and made images for them.

This led some exegetes to interpret the arrangement of the verse so that the referent of the pronoun in (*qalu*, "they said") is the polytheist Arabs, and that the mention of this in the midst of the story of the people of Noah is for the purpose of comparison. That is, the Arabs said to one another: "Do not abandon your gods, Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr," just as the people of Noah said to their followers, ﴿"Do not abandon your gods"﴾; then the mention returned after that to the people of Noah. This is clearly a forced reading and a disjointing of the parts of the arrangement of the speech.

The best view, which some exegetes have held and which we intend as the clarification, is that the idols of the people of Noah were effaced and the Flood overwhelmed them, but their names remained preserved among those who were saved with Noah from the believers. They mentioned them and admonished their young with what befell their forefathers as a consequence of worshipping those idols. So those names remained, and the early Arabs spoke of them in their traditions and reports. Then 'Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i came, who restored the worship of idols to the Arabs, and he named the idols for them with those names and others. Therefore the exegete has no need to digress into the attributes of the idols that had these names among the Arabs, nor into specifying the tribes that worshipped the referents of these names.

Further, it is possible that the people of Noah had many idols, which the saying of their great ones, ﴿"Do not abandon your gods"﴾, comprised; then they singled out the greatest of them by mention, and these are these five. In that case their mention is by specific-over-general (*'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm*), for the sake of attention to them, like God's words ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. It is also possible that they had no idols other than these five, in which case their mention in detail after the general statement is for the sake of attention to them, and the conjunction is of the type of synonymous conjunction (*'atf al-mura-dif*).

For the purpose of emphasis, the prohibitive verb was repeated, ﴿and do not abandon﴾, and the form of substitution was not followed. Lexical emphasis is sometimes combined with a conjunction, as in God's words ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgement is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 17], ﴿Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgement is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 18].

It is transmitted from al-Alusi, in the margin of his exegesis of this verse, this passage: The Europeans brought out, around the year 1260 (AH), idols and statues from the land of Mosul which were about three thousand years old.

The repetition of the negative particle (*la*, "not") in His words ﴿nor Suwa'﴾

[p. 210]

is to emphasize the negation expressed in ﴿do not abandon your gods﴾. The particle *la* is not repeated with ﴿Ya'uq and Nasr﴾, because the usage is that emphasis is not increased beyond three repetitions.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read (*wuddan*) with a *damma* on the *waw*. The others read it with a *fatha* on the *waw*. It is a non-Arabic proper name, which the Arabic language inflects however the speakers wish.

﴿Noah said: "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children have increased him only in loss. And they have plotted a great plot. And they have said: 'Do not abandon your gods, and do not abandon Wadd, or Suwa', or Yaghuth, or Ya'uq, or Nasr.'"﴾

They did so, but they were not worshipped until those men died and knowledge was forgotten, and then they were worshipped. It was also among Ghatafan, and An'um and A'la, who are from Tayy, and the people of Jarash from Madhhij, took it and brought it to Murad, and they worshipped it. Then the Banu Najiyah tried to remove it from A'la and An'um, so they fled with it to al-Husayn, brother of the Banu al-Harith of Khuza'ah. Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: I saw Yaghuth made of lead; they used to carry it on a camel that was *ahrad* (with a *ha'*, meaning one that paws with its forelegs when walking), and they would travel with it and not provoke it, until it was the one that knelt. Yaghuth was in the form of a lion.

Hamdan had an idol named Ya'uq, which was in the form of a horse. Kahlan of Saba' had it, and then his descendants inherited it until it came to Hamdan.

﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in misguidance﴾ may be the continuation of Nuh's speech, connected to the earlier report of his words. In that case the *waw* is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) joining part of a quoted sentence following the verb "he said" (*qāla*) to the part before it, in the way that objects are conjoined to one another, as when Imru' al-Qays says:

*Stop, let us weep*

Nuh concluded his complaint to God with a supplication against the misguided people he has been describing, asking that God increase them in misguidance.

Do not be troubled by the conjoining of a performative (*inshāʾ*) sentence to a declarative (*khabar*) one, because the prohibition on conjoining *inshāʾ* to *khabar* as an absolute rule is not sound, and the Qur'an is full of such usage.

It is also possible that the sentence ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in misguidance﴾ is not connected to the report of his words in ﴿He said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me"﴾ [Nuh: 21], but is the report of another statement of his, with an introduction in a different situation. In that case the *waw* conjoins one quoted sentence to another quoted sentence, standing in place of the verb "he said", as when you say: Imru' al-Qays said:

*Stop, let us weep*

and:

*Ah, good morning to you, O ruined encampment*

Those who refuse to conjoin *inshāʾ* to *khabar* have taken this view.

The intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" (*al-ẓālimīn*) is his people who disobeyed him. The apparent expectation would have been to refer to them by a pronoun referring back to "my people" in ﴿I have called my people night and day﴾ [Nuh: 5]. But he turned from the pronoun (*idmār*) to the explicit noun (*iẓhār*), contrary to what the apparent expectation requires, because the description of them as wrongdoers implies that they deserve to be deprived of God's care because of their wrongdoing, that is, their associating partners with God. So "wrongdoing" here means polytheism: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a tremendous wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

"Misguidance" (*ḍalāl*) is used figuratively for failing to find the way to the scheming that Nuh feared the harm of in ﴿And they schemed a great scheme﴾ [Nuh: 22]. That is: "Come between us and their scheming, and do not give them further respite in their transgression against us, except that You misguide them from their means." The exception here is of the type that affirms a thing by means of something resembling its opposite. Or he intended to conceal the paths of benefit to them, until their power is broken and their stubbornness softened, similar to the words of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88].

"Misguidance" does not mean straying from the path of truth and monotheism, since that clearly contradicts Nuh's call to his people to seek forgiveness and believe in the Resurrection. How, then, would he ask God to increase them in it?

It is also possible that "misguidance" was used to refer to the punishment caused by misguidance, that is, the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, which is the punishment of humiliation and pain.

It is also possible that the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*) and is part of God's speech to Nuh. In that case the *waw* is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyya*), and an omitted "saying" is understood: "And We said: do not increase the wrongdoers." The meaning is: do not increase them by calling them, for that will only increase them in misguidance. Thus the increase that comes from him increases them in disbelief and obstinacy. In this way "misguidance" remains in its well-known meaning in the terminology of the Qur'an, and the prohibitive form is used to express despair of his call benefiting them.

God informed Nuh that He would destroy them by His words ﴿They will be drowned, then they will be made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25], and the verse, which has the same meaning as His words ﴿It was revealed to Nuh that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not be distressed by what they do﴾ [Hud: 36] and ﴿Build the ship under Our eyes and Our revelation, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they will be drowned﴾ [Hud: 37].

Do you not see that the conclusions of both verses have the same meaning: His words here, "They will be drowned," and His words in the other verse, ﴿Indeed, they will be drowned﴾ [Hud: 37]?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 71, verse 25:

﴿Because of their sins they were drowned, and then they were made to enter the Fire, and they found for themselves no helpers besides Allah.﴾

Page 212

It is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridha) placed between the statements of Nuh, peace be upon him, and it is not part of the narration of Nuh's speech. Rather, it is an informing from Allah, exalted is He, to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) that He had decreed victory for Nuh and punishment for those of his people who disobeyed him, before Nuh asked Him to destroy them. The drowning of Nuh's people was therefore known to the Prophet (ﷺ); what is intended is informing him of its cause.

The purpose of this parenthetical insertion is to hasten the consolation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he encounters from his people, which is similar to what Nuh encountered from his people, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ [Ibrahim: 42].

It is also possible that it is connected to the phrase ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾ [Nuh: 24], according to the second aspect mentioned earlier, that it is part of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, addressed to Nuh, with the implied meaning: "And We said, do not increase the wrongdoers except in error." The past-tense form in His saying "were drowned" is then used to express the certainty of the promise to Nuh of their drowning. Likewise His saying ﴿and then they were made to enter the Fire﴾.

The phrase ﴿because of their sins﴾ has been placed before its governing verb to convey restriction (qasr), meaning: ﴿they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire﴾ because of the totality of their sins, not merely because of the response to Nuh's supplication that will be mentioned right after this, so that it is known that Allah does not allow His servants to persist in polytheism after He has sent them a messenger. Their punishment was delayed until after Nuh's supplication only to manifest his honor before his Lord among his people, as a source of joy for him and for the believers with him, and to hasten what could have been delayed.

The min (مِن) here is causal (ta'liliyya), and the ma (ما) is emphatic, reinforcing the sense of causation.

The plural "sins" (khati'at) is intended to include polytheism, denial of the Messenger, harming him, harming the believers with him, mocking him when he threatened them with the Flood, and all the crimes and abominations that these comprise.

Abu 'Amr alone read (khata'ayahum) as the plural of khatiyya, with the doubled ya' in which the ya' converted from a hamza is assimilated for lightening, while the majority (al-Jumhur) read khati'atihim in the plural form of khati'a with the hamza.

In His saying ﴿they were drowned and then they were made to enter the Fire﴾ there is the rhetorical embellishment of antithesis (tibaq), since between fire and drowning, which evokes water, there is opposition.

The consequential clause ﴿and they found for themselves no helpers besides Allah﴾ is an allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists among the Arabs

Page 213

who used to claim that the idols would intercede for them and ward off calamities from them, meaning in this world, since they did not believe in the Resurrection. That is: just as the idols did not help their worshippers among the people of Nuh, so too your idols will not help you.

The pronoun in "they found" refers to the wrongdoers in His saying ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾ [Nuh: 24], and likewise the pronoun in (lahum).

The meaning is: they did not find for themselves any helpers against the punishment of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 71, verses 26–27:

﴿And Noah said: "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller."﴾ ﴿"For indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked, ungrateful disbeliever."﴾ This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿Noah said: "My Lord, indeed they have disobeyed me"﴾ [Noah: 21]. He follows it with a supplication against them for their destruction and annihilation, by not leaving any of them alive; that is, "Do not leave any of them upon the earth."

The verb "said" (qāla) is repeated because a separation has occurred between Noah's statements by the clause ﴿because of their sins﴾ [Noah: 25] etc., or by it and the clause ﴿and do not increase the wrongdoers except in misguidance﴾ [Noah: 24]. It is joined by the conjunctive "wa" so that it stands independent and does not follow the clause ﴿indeed they have disobeyed me﴾ [Noah: 21], to indicate that Noah's supplication occurred after his complaint in his words ﴿indeed they have disobeyed me﴾ [Noah: 21].

Ayyār (dayyār): a word specifically used in negation, encompassing every person. It is a noun of the pattern fayʿāl derived from the noun "dār" (abode), its middle radical being a waw, because the middle radical of dār is presumed to be a waw. The original form of dayyār is daywār; when the waw and the yaʾ came together, were joined, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, the waw was changed into a yaʾ and then assimilated into the added yaʾ, as was done in sayyid and mayyit. The meaning of dayyār is one who dwells in the abode of a people, a metonym for a human being.

Similar to dayyār in generality and in use in negation are many nouns in the speech of the Arabs; the most extensive list is that of Ibn al-Sikkit in Iṣlāḥ al-Manṭiq, reaching twenty-five, and Kurāʿ al-Naml added seven, so they reached thirty-two nouns, and Ibn Mālik added six in al-Tashīl, so they became thirty-eight.

Among the most famous of them: aḥad, dayyār, and ʿarīb, all meaning a human being. The word (budd), with a dammah on the bāʾ and a shaddah on the unpointed dāl, means "separation" (mufāraqa).

The clause ﴿indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants﴾ is a justification for his request that God not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers; he means that he feared they would mislead some of the believers and that they would beget children who grow up upon their disbelief.

"The earth" (al-arḍ) may refer to the whole of the terrestrial globe, or to a specific land known to the speaker and addressee, as in His saying ﴿"Appoint me over the treasuries of the earth"﴾ [Yusuf: 55], meaning the land of Egypt in the Surah of Yusuf.

It is possible that humanity at that time was confined to the people of Noah, and it is also possible otherwise. On these possibilities arises the possibility that the Flood covered the entire terrestrial globe, and the possibility that it was a flood limited to a large region of the earth in general. And God knows best. This was already discussed in the explanation of His saying ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the ship﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 64] in the Surah of al-Aʿraf.

The predicate of "indeed" (innaka) is the whole conditional clause together with its response, which comes after "indeed"; for when a subject and a conditional come together, the conditional takes precedence over the subject, so the conditional is given the response and the subject is not given a predicate, because the conditional clause and its response indicate it.

Noah knew that they would beget only a wicked, ungrateful disbeliever by the fact that their children grow up among them, so they instil their religion in them and bar Noah from guiding them. Thus he gained knowledge of this matter by the evidence of experience.

The meaning: they will beget only one who becomes wicked and ungrateful upon reaching the age of reason.

Al-fājir: one characterised by wickedness (fujūr), which is the act of greatest corruption.

Al-kuffār: an intensive form of the one characterised by disbelief; that is, only one who combines bad conduct and bad belief. God the Exalted said ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [ʿAbasa: 42].

In Noah's speech there is an indication that reformers concern themselves with reforming their present generation and do not neglect laying the foundations for the reform of future generations, since all generations are equal in their reformist view. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb derived from God the Exalted's saying ﴿and those who came after them﴾ [al-Hashr: 10] evidence for leaving the land of Sawad of Iraq undivided among the army that conquered Iraq, making it a kharaj (land tax) for its people, with the aim of the continuance of provision from it for those Muslims who would come later.

﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents, and whoever enters my house as a believer, and the believing men and believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction.﴾

He placed the supplication for himself and his parents at the close of his intimate prayer. He began with himself, then with the people closest to him, who are his two parents. Then he generalized to his family and kin among the believers, so his children and grandchildren entered, and the believing women among their wives. He referred to them as "whoever enters my house" as a metaphor for their residing with him. Thus what is meant by his saying ﴿enters my house﴾ is a specific kind of entering, namely the frequent and constant entering. From this, a man's close associates are called his *dakhila* and *dukhla*. Then he generalized to the believing men and believing women. Then he returned to supplication against the disbelievers, asking that God deprive them of success. This is in the same manner as his earlier saying ﴿and do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾ [Nuh: 24].

*Al-tabar* means destruction and ruin. It is therefore a specification of the wrongdoers among his people, requesting their complete eradication after he had included them and others in the general statement ﴿Leave not upon the earth any of the disbelievers, a dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26], out of eagerness for the safety of human society from the taints of corruption and for its purification from the wicked elements.

*Walidahu* means his father and his mother. The name of his father appears in the Torah as "Lamak." As for his mother, al-Tha'labi mentioned that her name was Shamkha, daughter of Anush.

The majority of readers recited *(baytiya)* with the *sukun* on the first-person *ya'*. Hafs, from 'Asim, recited it with a *harakah* (vowel) on it.

The exception in ﴿except in destruction﴾ is *munqati'* (disjunctive), because destruction is not from the increase that he asked to be negated. He meant: do not increase them in wealth and children, because increasing these would give them strength to harm the believers. This is like the statement of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾ [Yunus: 88], and so on. This is from emphasizing a thing by means of what resembles its opposite, as in His saying ﴿but my call only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6].

Surah al-Jinn

It is called in the books of *tafsir* (exegesis) and in the codices we have seen, including the Kufic codex written in al-Qayrawan in the fifth century, "Surat al-Jinn." Likewise al-Tirmidhi titled it in the book of *tafsir* of his *Jami'*, and al-Bukhari titled it in the book of *tafsir* "Surat ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]."

It became well known among teachers and learners in the Qur'anic schools as "﴿Qul uhiya﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]."

Al-Suyuti did not mention it in *al-Itqan* among the surahs that have more than one name. The reason for both names is clear.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It appears that it was revealed around the tenth year of the Prophethood. In the two *Sahihs* and the *Jami'* of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ set out with a group
[Page 217]
of his companions, intending the market of 'Ukaz at Nakhla, and he was leading his companions in the dawn prayer. A group of the jinn listened to his recitation, and they returned to their people and said: 'We have heard a wondrous Qur'an.' And God revealed to His Prophet: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]."

Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the revelation of this surah was after the Messenger of God ﷺ's journey to al-Ta'if, seeking support from Thaqif. That would be in the tenth year after the Prophethood and the third year before the Hijrah.

The surah is counted as the fortieth in the order of revelation of surahs; it was revealed after al-A'raf and before Ya-Sin.

The scholars of counting agreed that its verses number twenty-eight.

* * *

Its purposes:

Establishing a miracle for the Prophet ﷺ, that his call reached the kind of the jinn, and that they understood meanings from the Qur'an that they heard from the Prophet ﷺ, and understood what he called to of monotheism and guidance, and their knowledge of the greatness of God and His transcendence above partners, consorts, and offspring.

Nullifying the worship of whatever is worshipped among the jinn.

Nullifying soothsaying, and the attainment of knowledge of the unseen by anyone other than the messengers whom God informs of what He wills.

Establishing that God has creatures called jinn, and that they are of kinds, among them the righteous and among them those below that rank by degrees; and refuting those who say about God what He has not said, those who worship the jinn, and those who deny resurrection; and that the jinn do not escape the authority of God, exalted is He.

Their wonder at being struck by the meteors of shooting stars that prevent eavesdropping. Regarding the purpose of this prevention and the escape from it, there is [a reference] to what God revealed to His Messenger ﷺ concerning the drought that afflicted the polytheists for their polytheism and for their preventing the mosques of God, and a warning to them that they would regret their conspiring against the Prophet ﷺ and their attempt to make him turn away from criticizing their religion.
